concept.name: Diagonal spread
concept.definition: A diagonal spread is a spread between two calls or two puts on the same underlying that differ in both strike price and expiration date — typically long a longer-dated option at one strike and short a shorter-dated option at a different strike. It combines the directional character of a vertical spread with the time-decay differential of a calendar spread.
concept.intuition: It is a calendar spread tilted with a directional view: the different strikes add a bullish or bearish lean to the front-month decay harvest.
concept.mechanics: Legs differ in strike and expiry, so the payoff depends on both the underlying's level and the term structure of volatility. A common structure, the diagonal call spread (long a longer-dated ITM call, short a near-dated OTM call), behaves like a leveraged covered call; maximum loss is limited to the net debit for the debit variants.
concept.failure_modes: The dual dependence on price and time makes outcomes hard to bound intuitively: big early moves, term-structure shifts, or early assignment of the short leg (especially before ex-dividend dates) can each undermine the position. Rolling the short leg repeatedly converts defined plans into path-dependent outcomes.
concept.misconceptions: A diagonal is not simply a cheaper covered call — unlike stock, the long option decays and can expire worthless, so the 'poor man's covered call' framing hides the long leg's own theta and vega risks.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, buy the 90-day $90 call for $12 and sell the 30-day $105 call for $1.50: net debit $10.50. If XYZ drifts to $104 by the short leg's expiry, the short call decays while the long call keeps most of its value.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
